meetingTitle: Raffles Place Flagship & App Promo Launch

card.youAre: You are Wei Ling, Operations Director looking after the shop floor, Auntie Mary, food hygiene, and the budget.
facts: Our 28-seat Raffles Place shop has four 4-seater booths (16 seats) with 12 wall sockets and free guest Wi-Fi, plus six 2-seater tables.
Four freelancers held the 4-seater booths for two hours every morning this week on a single $2.20 drink, costing about $420 a morning in lost breakfast sets.

Auntie Mary (62) is the only floor staff who seats solo diners with hot trays and clears tables. A customer in a suit shouted at her last week when she moved his tissue packet, and she will not police seats or touch customers' belongings.
60% of our morning customers dine solo and cannot carry a hot tray of runny soft-boiled eggs without a table.

Our internal counter hygiene SOP keeps money handling separate from ready-to-eat food: anyone who touches coins or notes must change gloves and wash hands before slicing toast (+40s per order). Counting the cash float at night costs $380 a month in overtime.
The toast counter runs on two staff at the 8am rush, so there is no spare pair of hands to take cash and make change without slowing toast orders.
Wholesale Anchor salted butter went up 35% last month. Doubling the 12g slab to 20g on every set adds $0.42 a set, about $1,100 a month in margin.
We have $750 left in the launch promo budget.
card.responsibility: Make sure our plans work for Auntie Mary and the counter staff without breaking food hygiene or blowing our margin.

card.youAre: You are Arjun, Tech & POS Lead looking after the self-order kiosks, the kitchen docket printer, and store power.
facts: The 15-inch kiosk screen fits 12 drink buttons per page and about 18 characters per line.

The kitchen docket currently prints the same button name the customer sees, so renaming a button changes what the kitchen reads. POS v2.4 can hold a separate kitchen print name, but it has to be configured and tested before the morning rush.
When English names printed on kitchen dockets at Tampines, our 65-year-old kopi uncles slowed down by 15 seconds a cup.
The 12 booth wall sockets and guest Wi-Fi run on a programmable smart relay breaker in the back room. Cutting power also hits paying customers using the sockets.
Physical cash bill-acceptors for the kiosks cost $1,400 and take 3 weeks to arrive. There is no spare till or cashier terminal at the front.
The kiosks can take cards and PayNow tomorrow, but not cash.
POS changes made tonight still need a short kitchen test before 8am.
card.responsibility: Keep the kiosks, kitchen printer, and store power simple enough to configure and test tonight.

card.youAre: You are Mei, Menu & Store Experience Lead looking after our kopi and kaya toast recipes, the menu, and customer flow.
facts: In yesterday's Raffles Place trial, 19 of 28 first-time kiosk users froze for over 2 minutes at 'Kopi O Kosong', 'Kopi C Siew Dai' or 'Teh Halia', and 72% missed the small corner language toggle.
Our retired morning regulars carry $2 and $10 notes, so a $2.20 Kopi always needs change. Yesterday 14 of them walked out when asked to use a $20 minimum stored-value card instead.
60% of our morning crowd dines solo while carrying hot trays of runny soft-boiled eggs.
Our 12g cold butter slab did not shrink: it stays thick on dine-in open plates, but melts flat inside a closed takeaway box with hot toast.
A separate chilled butter cup costs $0.05 a box, and a steam-vented takeaway box is also available; both keep the same 12g slab.
Local regulars mocked a rival kopitiam on Reddit when it renamed Kopi O to 'Local Americano'.
card.responsibility: Keep our kopi and kaya toast authentic while making ordering and finding a seat easier.

card.youAre: You are Daniel, Marketing Lead looking after TikTok reviews, store promos, and public goodwill.
facts: Food TikToker @MakanWithZack (85k followers) posted a reel titled 'Did Nanyang Kopi shrink their butter slice?!' that already has 90,000 views.
Zack offered to film an 8:30am live re-taste tomorrow for $600 cash, or $450 cash plus 20 Kaya Toast plushie keychains from our storeroom.
Zack warned that his followers will check whether regular customers get the exact same portion he is served.
A TikTok clip of a 74-year-old regular turned away at our 'NO CASH ACCEPTED' sign has 40,000 views calling us anti-elderly.
Google reviews dropped to 3.6 stars during our soft trial because breakfast walk-ins could not find a seat while laptop campers held the 4-seater booths for two hours.
card.responsibility: Win back public goodwill on TikTok without promising things the kitchen cannot deliver for every customer.

card.youAre: You are Sam, General Manager chairing the huddle.
facts: Call on the lead for each topic and let the team hash out the practical catches.
Make sure each topic wraps up with a clear call and someone owning the follow-up.
card.responsibility: Chair the huddle, hear both sides out, and assign a follow-up owner for each topic.

agenda.title: First-timers stalling at the kiosk over Kopi names
agenda.decision: how do we help first-time customers order Kopi confidently without slowing the kitchen or losing our kopitiam identity?

openingViews.view: First-timers freeze because the kiosk assumes they already know Kopi shorthand. We should make the drink choices easier to understand without hiding our own names.
Every extra label or screen we add has to survive the 15-inch, 12-button grid and the kitchen docket, so I do not want a change that makes the kitchen read long English names.

tradeOffs.tradeOff: 19 of 28 first-time trial users froze at Kopi O Kosong and 72% missed the corner language toggle; a fix that only adds a toggle leaves most people stuck.
tradeOffs.question: What does a first-timer actually see at the moment they have to choose a drink?

tradeOffs.tradeOff: The kitchen docket prints the same button name the customer sees, and the 12-button grid leaves no room for long two-line labels on one page.
tradeOffs.question: How do we keep the kitchen ticket readable without pushing half the menu onto a second page?

tradeOffs.tradeOff: The kopi uncles read shorthand at a glance; a slow docket costs 15 seconds a cup at the morning rush and there is no spare hand to help them.
tradeOffs.question: Who absorbs the extra time if the kitchen has to interpret new labels?

agenda.title: Morning seat crunch & laptop campers
agenda.decision: how do we free up tables for breakfast diners without turning Auntie Mary into seat police or punishing solo customers?

openingViews.view: The morning floor is losing tables to tissue-packet reservations and laptop campers, and Auntie Mary cannot be the one who confronts customers.
Most of our morning customers are solo diners carrying hot trays. Any rule that makes them wait longer for a seat hurts the people we are trying to protect.

tradeOffs.tradeOff: Four 4-seater booths (16 of 28 seats) are held for two hours by freelancers on one $2.20 drink, costing about $420 a morning, and Auntie Mary was shouted at the last time she moved a tissue packet.
tradeOffs.question: Who enforces any new seating rule if it cannot be Auntie Mary?

tradeOffs.tradeOff: 60% of morning customers dine solo and cannot carry a hot tray of runny eggs without a table; a blanket ban on reserving seats leaves them standing with hot food.
tradeOffs.question: Where does a solo diner with a hot tray sit while the queue clears?

tradeOffs.tradeOff: The booth sockets and guest Wi-Fi run on a smart relay breaker, but cutting power is a blunt tool that also hits paying customers and can look petty online.
tradeOffs.question: Is the answer power, layout or timing, and what evidence will tell us it worked?

agenda.title: Elderly regulars turned away at cashless kiosks
agenda.decision: how do we let retired regulars pay with cash without breaking our counter hygiene or forcing them into prepayment?

openingViews.view: The kiosks cannot take cash tomorrow. The hardware is expensive and slow to arrive, so I need a plan that works with the equipment we already have.
Our counter hygiene rule exists for a reason: the toast staff cannot handle money and ready-to-eat food in the same pair of gloves.

tradeOffs.tradeOff: Money and ready-to-eat food must stay separate: staff who touch coins or notes must change gloves and wash hands before slicing toast, adding 40 seconds per order, and nightly float counting costs $380 a month in overtime.
tradeOffs.question: Who runs the cash point, and how are change and payment counted and balanced at close?

tradeOffs.tradeOff: Physical kiosk cash acceptors cost $1,400 and take three weeks, and the front has no spare till or cashier terminal.
tradeOffs.question: What can take cash tomorrow without new hardware or a second queue?

tradeOffs.tradeOff: A 74-year-old regular was filmed being turned away and the clip has 40,000 views; 94% of the regulars who walked out carry only $2 or $10 notes, so a $2.20 Kopi needs change.
tradeOffs.question: How do we make the fix visible and simple enough that no regular has to download an app or prepay $20?

agenda.title: @MakanWithZack's TikTok on our butter slice
agenda.decision: how should we answer @MakanWithZack's butter video and tomorrow's re-taste without faking portions or blowing our margin?

openingViews.view: This video is painting us as stingy. We need a visible response tomorrow, not a quiet correction.
The butter did not shrink; our takeaway packing is melting it. Doubling every slice would punish the kitchen and our margin for a problem that may be in the box.

tradeOffs.tradeOff: The 12g slab stays thick on dine-in open plates but melts flat in a closed takeaway box with hot toast; any fix has to keep the same standard for every customer.
tradeOffs.question: What do we change so the customer sees the butter we actually serve?

tradeOffs.tradeOff: Anchor salted butter is up 35%; doubling to 20g on every set costs $0.42 a set, about $1,100 a month, and we only have $750 left in the launch budget.
tradeOffs.question: What can we spend on a response, and what are we willing to change permanently?

tradeOffs.tradeOff: Zack wants $600 cash, or $450 with 20 plushies, for an 8:30am live re-taste, and his followers will check whether regular customers get the same portion.
tradeOffs.question: What do we show on camera, and how do we prove it is the standard every customer gets?

tradeOffs.tradeOff: Regular customers queue right behind Zack; an influencer-only portion or a secret button will be seen and will backfire.
tradeOffs.question: How do we make any change visible and consistent at the counter?
